newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Court of Appeals backs Columbus in bond case.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Court of Appeals backs Columbus in bond case.

text.p: The U.S. Court of Appeals in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday ruled for Columbus, Ohio, in the city's dispute with the Internal Revenue Service over the tax status of a city bond issue.

Columbus had sought to issue $27.3 million of refunding bonds with tax-exempt status to pay off notes it had issued to satisfy a 1967 obligation to the state pension funds, attorney David Rogers said.
An IRS private letter in 1994 denied the tax exemption, however, finding that the issue would be arbitrage bonds and not eligible for tax exemption.
A U.S. Tax Court judge upheld that decision, following a Columbus appeal and the city sought further review.
A three-judge panel found that the Tax Court erred in finding that the city had, in effect, prepaid for proerty it had acquired, vacating the ruling and remanded for further consideration.
The IRS has 14 days to seek a rehearing of the decision before the Court of Appeals.

"We feel that the logic of the opinion written by the Court of Appeals indicates that the Tax Court should find in our favor and we should have a final resolution that allows the city to issue its bonds in the near future," Rogers said.
Columbus had unfunded pension funds for its police and firefighters when Ohio created a fully-funded statewide fund and determined that the city's contribution to the state should be $42.7 million.

In 1993, Columbus won passage of a bill in the Ohio legislature permitting prepayment of the liabilities in return for a discount. The contribution owed was reduced to $27 million under that plan and the city sought to issue tax-exempt general obligation bonds.
Columbus paid the principal owed, plus interest, using bond anticipation notes due to mature Jan. 30, 1998. If the city prevails, it plans to refund the notes with tax-exempt GO bonds.
If it stands, six to 12 other Ohio municipalities could stand to benefit from the ruling, which is specific to the state, Rogers said.
"It's certainly not final, but we are very pleased with the decision," Rogers said.
